title: Traits need turning (7:3)
hookLine: return is needed not only for acts but for anger, envy and jealousy
tomorrow: after years of messing up, are you at the back of the line?

lines: TEN AT NIGHT. A MISSED CUE.
THE ACT, OR WHAT'S UNDER IT?
cards: Thursday rehearsal, ten at night. The stage manager has a clipboard, a headset and no patience left, and the freshman on the light board just missed the same cue again.
She snaps, loud enough that the whole cast goes quiet. Later she texts him: sorry i yelled, that was out of line. He sends back a thumbs-up.
Apology made, slate clean. Except she knows something he doesn't. This isn't the first time this month, and it was never really about the cue.
The yelling was one act. The thing underneath has been there all year. So which one does she return from?

teach.b: Maimonides answers in chapter seven of his laws of return, and it reads like a turn in the plot. Until now, the examples have been deeds: something you did, that you can stop doing.

Then he writes: don't say that teshuvah is only for sins with an act in them, like theft or robbery. Just as a person must turn from those, they must search out the bad traits they carry and turn from them too.
And he names them: anger, hatred, jealousy, mockery, chasing money and honor, chasing food. Then a line you might not expect in a law book.

teach.h: HARDER THAN THE SINS OF ACTION.
teach.b: These, he says, are harder than the sins of action, because once a person is sunk in a trait, it's hard to get out. A theft happens on one day. A temper comes along to every day of the week.

teach.h: FORSAKE THE WAY, AND THE THOUGHTS.
teach.b: He backs it with Isaiah: "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the man of iniquity his thoughts." The way is the road you walk. The thoughts are where the walking starts.

Here's the thing worth repeating tonight: in this book, a short fuse isn't a personality. It's a project, something you turn slowly, the way you'd steer a ship, not flip a switch. And the apology still matters.
Repair is real. It just isn't the whole job. The act gets an apology.

how: Jewish ethical practice, sometimes called mussar, works on one trait at a time; in the weeks before Yom Kippur Jews traditionally take stock of their character as well as their deeds.

o: only deeds need return; your nature is fixed
a habit must be broken before an apology counts
the habits under our acts need return as well

games.q: what's in chapter seven — tap the pairs.
p: the traits, once you're sunk in them
forsake the way, and the thoughts

s: a sincere apology for an outburst completes the return for a temper
the act gets repaired. Maimonides says the trait underneath needs its own turning.
Maimonides calls traits harder to leave than sins of action
once a person is sunk in a trait, he writes, it's hard to get out.
in this law book, return is only about deeds
chapter seven adds anger, hatred, jealousy, mockery and more.

games.q: a friend keeps borrowing five dollars and 'forgetting.' each time he apologizes and pays it back. what would Maimonides look at?
o: each loan on its own; every repayment closes that case.
the habit under the loans, which needs its own turning.
nothing more; he paid it all back, so it's settled.
games.why: the repayments are real repair. but chapter seven says to search out the trait under the acts, and calls that the harder work.

practice: Find a scrap of paper and a pen. Write the name of one trait you'd like to turn, just the word: impatience, envy, the need to win. Under it, write one moment this week when it showed up.
Then sit with the page and ask it, without scolding, what it's trying to protect.

wordCard.voice: Traits need turning: return isn't only for what you did, but for the anger, envy and jealousy underneath. Maimonides calls those the harder ones.

orig.note: Hebrew: dispositions, a person's traits; the word Maimonides uses for them here.

carryVoice: For the road: traits need turning too, since the act gets an apology and the trait gets time. Eighteen of thirty.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 7:3 (return from traits as well as acts; anger, hatred, jealousy, mockery, chasing money, honor and food; harder than sins of action)
